character.centerRule: Noah remains the center only where a bounded source materially develops his identity, household, action, speech, ancestry, or later canonical reception. Flood, covenant, water, judgment, and descendants retain their own subject boundaries.

phases.orientation: Noah is named within a genealogy, becomes a father, and is distinguished inside a world described as corrupt and violent.
phases.title: Name and world

phases.orientation: God announces judgment, gives Noah detailed instructions, and the narrative follows his obedience into the flood.
phases.title: Warning and the ship

phases.orientation: God remembers Noah and the animals, the waters recede, the household leaves the ship, and worship meets a changed divine commitment.
phases.title: Remembered and restored

phases.orientation: Blessing, blood accountability, covenant, vineyard exposure, family speech, nations, and death shape life after the flood.
phases.title: Blessing and household fracture

phases.orientation: Genealogy, prophecy, wisdom, prayer, and analogy remember Noah for ancestry, righteousness, preservation, covenant, and endurance.
phases.title: Ancestry and later memory

phases.orientation: Jesus and apostolic writers reuse Noah through unexpected judgment, faith, rescue, water, baptism, righteousness, and future warning.
phases.title: Warning, faith, and water

character.throughline: The trail moves from name and generation through warning, obedience, preservation, remembered dry ground, worship, blessing, covenant, family fracture, death, ancestry, and later interpretation.

leftEvidence.title: Lamech names Noah in hope of comfort

points.label: Noah-relative action
points.left: Lamech names his son Noah while speaking of work, painful toil, and the ground the LORD cursed.
points.right: Noah builds an altar and offers from every clean animal and bird.

points.label: Response and consequence
points.left: The genealogy then names Noah as father of Shem, Ham, and Japheth.
points.right: The LORD smells the aroma and resolves not to strike all living things again, even while naming human evil from youth.

compares.posture: Lamech speaks of comfort from cursed-ground toil; after Noah’s offering, the LORD promises continuing seasons and limits another strike against all life.

rightEvidence.title: Noah builds an altar after leaving the ship

compares.tension: The later divine resolve answers part of the ground problem without declaring human inclination repaired.
compares.title: Comfort hoped for and the ground after the flood

leftEvidence.title: Noah finds favor in a violent world

points.label: Noah-relative action
points.left: The LORD sees continual human evil and a corrupt earth filled with violence; Noah finds favor and is called righteous and blameless among his contemporaries.
points.right: Noah receives warning about unseen things, responds with godly fear, and prepares a ship for his household.

points.label: Response and consequence
points.left: Noah walks with God and fathers three sons while the earth’s corruption is repeatedly named.
points.right: The verse says this condemned the world and made Noah an heir of righteousness according to faith.

compares.posture: Genesis names favor, righteousness, blamelessness, and walking with God; Hebrews names faith, godly fear, action, and inherited righteousness.

rightEvidence.title: Hebrews interprets Noah’s response as faith

compares.tension: The descriptions overlap around Noah but belong to different writers and cannot be collapsed into one vocabulary.
compares.title: Noah described in Genesis and Hebrews

leftEvidence.title: Noah receives warning and ship instructions

points.label: Noah-relative action
points.left: God tells Noah that violence has brought an end to all flesh, then specifies the ship, its rooms, dimensions, covering, occupants, animals, and food.
points.right: Noah receives warning about unseen things, responds with godly fear, and prepares a ship for his household.

points.label: Response and consequence
points.left: Noah does everything God commands after receiving a covenant announcement about entering with his household.
points.right: The verse says this condemned the world and made Noah an heir of righteousness according to faith.

compares.posture: Genesis records God’s warning, detailed command, and Noah’s obedience; Hebrews interprets the response to unseen warning as faith.

rightEvidence.title: Hebrews interprets Noah’s response as faith

compares.tension: Later interpretation adds a stated inner posture without turning it into a quotation from Noah.
compares.title: Commanded work and faith toward the unseen

leftEvidence.title: Noah’s household enters before the rain

points.label: Noah-relative action
points.left: The LORD tells Noah to enter with his household, distinguishes clean and unclean animals, and announces seven days before forty days of rain.
points.right: Jesus says the day and hour are unknown and compares the Son of Man’s coming with ordinary life continuing until Noah entered the ship.

points.label: Response and consequence
points.left: Noah obeys; his family and the animals enter as the flood approaches.
points.right: The flood arrives unexpectedly, and the comparison leads to watchfulness and readiness.

compares.posture: Genesis counts the days and narrates Noah’s entry; Matthew makes that entry the boundary before unexpected judgment.

rightEvidence.title: Jesus compares his coming with Noah’s days

compares.tension: A known seven-day interval in Noah’s story becomes an analogy for an hour no one knows in Matthew’s teaching.
compares.title: Entering the ship and the unexpected day

leftEvidence.title: The LORD shuts Noah in as the flood rises

points.label: Noah-relative action
points.left: The fountains and windows open; Noah, his household, and living creatures enter, and the LORD shuts him in.
points.right: The prayer recalls human ungodliness, flood destruction, and Noah being left with his household and righteous descendants.

points.label: Response and consequence
points.left: The waters rise until all dry-land life outside dies; only Noah and those with him remain.
points.right: Adam’s death and the flood are set in a recurring history of corruption.

compares.posture: Genesis says only Noah and those with him remain; 2 Esdras remembers Noah with his household and righteous descendants.

rightEvidence.title: A prayer remembers Noah’s household after worldwide death

compares.tension: The later prayer interprets the preserved line while Genesis’ bounded flood scene simply identifies those left alive.

leftEvidence.title: God remembers Noah as the waters recede

points.label: Noah-relative action
points.left: God remembers Noah and the animals, sends a wind, and restrains the waters; Noah later opens the window and sends a raven and a dove.
points.right: God establishes a covenant with Noah, his sons, their offspring, every living creature, and the earth.

points.label: Response and consequence
points.left: Noah waits through repeated intervals, reads the olive leaf, removes the covering, and sees dry ground.
points.right: The rainbow is named as the sign God will see and remember when clouds gather.

compares.posture: Genesis 8 begins with God remembering Noah and the animals; Genesis 9 repeatedly attaches remembering to the rainbow covenant.
compares.tension: The same verb serves rescue in one scene and an enduring promise concerning all flesh in another.
compares.title: God remembers Noah and promises to remember the covenant

points.label: Noah-relative action
points.left: God tells Noah to leave with his household and bring out every living creature so life can multiply on earth.
points.right: God blesses Noah and his sons, commands fruitfulness, permits animal food, forbids consuming life with blood, and requires an account for human blood.

points.label: Response and consequence
points.left: Noah, his family, and the creatures leave after their families.
points.right: The image of God grounds the statement about human bloodshed.

compares.posture: Noah leaves with his household and the creatures under a command to multiply; the following blessing repeats fruitfulness while changing food, fear, and blood accountability.

rightEvidence.title: Noah receives blessing and blood commands

compares.tension: Renewed creation language preserves continuity while the human-animal relation is not simply restored to its earlier form.
compares.title: Leaving the ship and receiving a new-world blessing

leftEvidence.title: Noah builds an altar after leaving the ship

points.label: Noah-relative action
points.left: Noah builds an altar and offers from every clean animal and bird.
points.right: God establishes a covenant with Noah, his sons, their offspring, every living creature, and the earth.

points.label: Response and consequence
points.left: The LORD smells the aroma and resolves not to strike all living things again, even while naming human evil from youth.
points.right: The rainbow is named as the sign God will see and remember when clouds gather.

compares.posture: The altar scene records a divine resolve about the ground and seasons; the next covenant scene names descendants, creatures, earth, and the rainbow.
compares.tension: The narrative joins the scenes in sequence while preserving distinct speech, scope, and sign.

leftEvidence.title: The LORD shuts Noah in as the flood rises

points.label: Noah-relative action
points.left: The fountains and windows open; Noah, his household, and living creatures enter, and the LORD shuts him in.
points.right: Across famine, animals, sword, and pestilence, Noah is named with Daniel and Job as a righteous person who could deliver only himself.

points.label: Response and consequence
points.left: The waters rise until all dry-land life outside dies; only Noah and those with him remain.
points.right: Even sons and daughters would not be delivered by the presence of those righteous people in the judged land.

compares.posture: Genesis preserves Noah’s household in the ship; Ezekiel imagines Noah able to deliver only himself in another judged land.

rightEvidence.title: Ezekiel limits what Noah’s righteousness can deliver

compares.tension: The texts use Noah in different judgment settings, so neither statement can be made to erase the other.
compares.title: A household saved and righteousness limited

points.label: Noah-relative action
points.left: God establishes a covenant with Noah, his sons, their offspring, every living creature, and the earth.
points.right: The LORD compares a promise not to remain angry with the oath that Noah’s waters will not again cover the earth.

points.label: Response and consequence
points.left: The rainbow is named as the sign God will see and remember when clouds gather.
points.right: Covenant peace and enduring kindness are set against mountains and hills that may move.

compares.posture: Genesis names the covenant with Noah, descendants, creatures, and earth; Isaiah invokes Noah’s waters inside a promise of unremoved peace.

rightEvidence.title: Isaiah remembers the waters of Noah

compares.tension: Isaiah receives the flood limit as precedent while authoring a new promise in a new setting.
compares.title: Flood covenant and covenant-of-peace memory

leftEvidence.title: Noah’s vineyard exposes a household fracture

points.label: Noah-relative action
points.left: Noah plants a vineyard, becomes drunk, and lies uncovered; Ham sees and reports, while Shem and Japheth cover without looking.
points.right: Sirach calls Noah perfect and righteous and says he kept the race alive in a season of wrath.

points.label: Response and consequence
points.left: After waking, Noah speaks a curse over Canaan and blessings concerning Shem and Japheth, then the account closes with his death.
points.right: Everlasting covenants and the limit on another flood complete the short remembrance.

compares.posture: Genesis ends Noah’s life with drunken exposure, family response, speech, and death; Sirach remembers perfect righteousness, remnant, and covenant.

rightEvidence.title: Sirach remembers Noah as righteous and preserving a remnant

compares.tension: The compact praise is true to its selected purpose without functioning as a complete biography.
compares.title: Household fracture and remembered righteousness

leftEvidence.title: Chronicles places Noah between Adam and his sons

points.label: Noah-relative action
points.left: Chronicles opens with a compressed chain from Adam to Noah and then names Shem, Ham, and Japheth.
points.right: Luke’s genealogy moves backward from Jesus through David and Abraham to Noah, Lamech, Adam, and God.

points.label: Response and consequence
points.left: The long flood narrative is reduced to Noah’s place in ancestral succession.
points.right: Noah is one link in a lineage with a direction and endpoint different from Chronicles.

compares.posture: Chronicles moves from Adam toward Noah and his sons; Luke moves backward from Jesus through Noah to Adam and God.

rightEvidence.title: Luke places Noah in Jesus’ ancestry

compares.tension: Both place Noah in ancestry, but their direction and literary purpose differ.
compares.title: Noah in two genealogical directions

leftEvidence.title: The families of Noah’s sons become nations

points.label: Noah-relative action
points.left: The genealogy traces peoples, lands, languages, cities, and nations through Shem, Ham, and Japheth.
points.right: Chronicles opens with a compressed chain from Adam to Noah and then names Shem, Ham, and Japheth.

points.label: Response and consequence
points.left: Noah remains the ancestral point while the descendants become distinct families and peoples.
points.right: The long flood narrative is reduced to Noah’s place in ancestral succession.

compares.posture: Genesis unfolds families, languages, lands, and nations from Noah’s sons; Chronicles compresses the same generational hinge into four names.

rightEvidence.title: Chronicles places Noah between Adam and his sons

compares.tension: The sources preserve the same ancestry at radically different narrative scales.
compares.title: Nations from Noah’s sons and a compressed ancestral line

leftEvidence.title: Noah receives warning and ship instructions

points.label: Noah-relative action
points.left: God tells Noah that violence has brought an end to all flesh, then specifies the ship, its rooms, dimensions, covering, occupants, animals, and food.
points.right: The writer compares a mother enduring her children’s torment to Noah’s ship bearing up in the world-filling flood.

points.label: Response and consequence
points.left: Noah does everything God commands after receiving a covenant announcement about entering with his household.
points.right: Flood, waves, storms, and preservation become poetic language for disciplined endurance.

compares.posture: Genesis describes Noah building a ship for preservation; 4 Maccabees turns that ship into an analogy for a mother enduring overwhelming grief.

rightEvidence.title: Noah’s ship becomes an image of endurance

compares.tension: The analogy depends on the ship’s flood setting without making the two human stories identical.
compares.title: The commanded ship and a later endurance image

leftEvidence.title: Tobit includes Noah in ancestral marriage advice

points.label: Noah-relative action

points.right: Noah plants a vineyard, becomes drunk, and lies uncovered; Ham sees and reports, while Shem and Japheth cover without looking.

points.label: Response and consequence
points.left: Blessing in children and inheritance are attached to the remembered ancestors.
points.right: After waking, Noah speaks a curse over Canaan and blessings concerning Shem and Japheth, then the account closes with his death.

compares.posture: Tobit presents Noah as an ancestral marriage example; Genesis names Noah’s wife but gives no account of her family origin.

rightEvidence.title: Noah’s vineyard exposes a household fracture

compares.tension: The later advice makes a claim whose supporting detail is not narrated in the earlier household scene.
compares.title: Tobit’s ancestral advice and Genesis’ household record

leftEvidence.title: Jesus compares his coming with Noah’s days

points.label: Noah-relative action
points.left: Jesus says the day and hour are unknown and compares the Son of Man’s coming with ordinary life continuing until Noah entered the ship.
points.right: Jesus compares the future day with Noah’s days of ordinary activity until the flood and with Lot’s departure before destruction.

points.label: Response and consequence
points.left: The flood arrives unexpectedly, and the comparison leads to watchfulness and readiness.
points.right: The saying moves into warnings not to turn back and questions about loss, preservation, and location.

compares.posture: Both Gospels connect ordinary activity, Noah’s entry, and sudden destruction to the Son of Man.

rightEvidence.title: Luke places Noah beside Lot in teaching about the Son of Man

compares.tension: Matthew develops watchfulness and the unknown hour; Luke pairs Noah with Lot and develops departure, loss, and not turning back.
compares.title: The days of Noah in Matthew and Luke

leftEvidence.title: The LORD shuts Noah in as the flood rises

points.label: Noah-relative action
points.left: The fountains and windows open; Noah, his household, and living creatures enter, and the LORD shuts him in.
points.right: Christ’s suffering, death, life in the Spirit, proclamation to imprisoned spirits, divine patience, Noah’s ship, eight people, and water appear in one compressed sequence.

points.label: Response and consequence
points.left: The waters rise until all dry-land life outside dies; only Noah and those with him remain.
points.right: Baptism is called a corresponding figure and is distinguished from bodily dirt removal through conscience, resurrection, and Christ’s exaltation.

compares.posture: Genesis narrates water destroying outside life while the ship preserves Noah’s household; 1 Peter carries Noah’s water into a statement about baptism through Christ’s resurrection.

rightEvidence.title: Peter carries Noah’s water into a difficult baptism argument

compares.tension: The correspondence is explicit, but the passage itself rejects a simple bodily-washing explanation and leaves difficult links open.
compares.title: Flood preservation and baptismal correspondence

leftEvidence.title: Noah receives warning and ship instructions

points.label: Noah-relative action
points.left: God tells Noah that violence has brought an end to all flesh, then specifies the ship, its rooms, dimensions, covering, occupants, animals, and food.
points.right: Noah and seven others are preserved while the ancient world is judged; the passage also remembers angels, Sodom, Gomorrah, and Lot.

points.label: Response and consequence
points.left: Noah does everything God commands after receiving a covenant announcement about entering with his household.
points.right: These examples support the claim that the Lord knows how to deliver the godly and reserve the unrighteous for judgment.

compares.posture: Genesis records command and obedience without a sermon; 2 Peter names Noah a preacher of righteousness.

rightEvidence.title: Peter calls Noah a preacher of righteousness

compares.tension: The later title is canonical evidence about Noah but cannot be rewritten as speech supplied by Genesis.
compares.title: Noah obeys and later becomes a preacher

compares.posture: 1 Peter places Noah inside a Christ, spirits, water, and baptism sequence; 2 Peter places him inside examples of judgment and deliverance.

rightEvidence.title: Peter calls Noah a preacher of righteousness

compares.tension: The shared Noah memory supports different arguments and should not be forced into one explanation.
compares.title: Two apostolic uses of Noah

edges.basis: Lamech speaks of comfort from cursed-ground toil; after Noah’s offering, the LORD promises continuing seasons and limits another strike against all life. The later divine resolve answers part of the ground problem without declaring human inclination repaired.
edges.label: Comfort hoped for and the ground after the flood

edges.basis: Genesis names favor, righteousness, blamelessness, and walking with God; Hebrews names faith, godly fear, action, and inherited righteousness. The descriptions overlap around Noah but belong to different writers and cannot be collapsed into one vocabulary.
edges.label: Noah described in Genesis and Hebrews

edges.basis: Genesis records God’s warning, detailed command, and Noah’s obedience; Hebrews interprets the response to unseen warning as faith. Later interpretation adds a stated inner posture without turning it into a quotation from Noah.
edges.label: Commanded work and faith toward the unseen

edges.basis: Genesis counts the days and narrates Noah’s entry; Matthew makes that entry the boundary before unexpected judgment. A known seven-day interval in Noah’s story becomes an analogy for an hour no one knows in Matthew’s teaching.
edges.label: Entering the ship and the unexpected day

edges.basis: Genesis says only Noah and those with him remain; 2 Esdras remembers Noah with his household and righteous descendants. The later prayer interprets the preserved line while Genesis’ bounded flood scene simply identifies those left alive.
edges.label: The household preserved and later remembered

edges.basis: Genesis 8 begins with God remembering Noah and the animals; Genesis 9 repeatedly attaches remembering to the rainbow covenant. The same verb serves rescue in one scene and an enduring promise concerning all flesh in another.
edges.label: God remembers Noah and promises to remember the covenant

edges.basis: Noah leaves with his household and the creatures under a command to multiply; the following blessing repeats fruitfulness while changing food, fear, and blood accountability. Renewed creation language preserves continuity while the human-animal relation is not simply restored to its earlier form.
edges.label: Leaving the ship and receiving a new-world blessing

edges.basis: The altar scene records a divine resolve about the ground and seasons; the next covenant scene names descendants, creatures, earth, and the rainbow. The narrative joins the scenes in sequence while preserving distinct speech, scope, and sign.
edges.label: Altar response and covenant speech

edges.basis: Genesis preserves Noah’s household in the ship; Ezekiel imagines Noah able to deliver only himself in another judged land. The texts use Noah in different judgment settings, so neither statement can be made to erase the other.
edges.label: A household saved and righteousness limited

edges.basis: Genesis names the covenant with Noah, descendants, creatures, and earth; Isaiah invokes Noah’s waters inside a promise of unremoved peace. Isaiah receives the flood limit as precedent while authoring a new promise in a new setting.
edges.label: Flood covenant and covenant-of-peace memory

edges.basis: Genesis ends Noah’s life with drunken exposure, family response, speech, and death; Sirach remembers perfect righteousness, remnant, and covenant. The compact praise is true to its selected purpose without functioning as a complete biography.
edges.label: Household fracture and remembered righteousness

edges.basis: Chronicles moves from Adam toward Noah and his sons; Luke moves backward from Jesus through Noah to Adam and God. Both place Noah in ancestry, but their direction and literary purpose differ.
edges.label: Noah in two genealogical directions

edges.basis: Genesis unfolds families, languages, lands, and nations from Noah’s sons; Chronicles compresses the same generational hinge into four names. The sources preserve the same ancestry at radically different narrative scales.
edges.label: Nations from Noah’s sons and a compressed ancestral line

edges.basis: Genesis describes Noah building a ship for preservation; 4 Maccabees turns that ship into an analogy for a mother enduring overwhelming grief. The analogy depends on the ship’s flood setting without making the two human stories identical.
edges.label: The commanded ship and a later endurance image

edges.basis: Tobit presents Noah as an ancestral marriage example; Genesis names Noah’s wife but gives no account of her family origin. The later advice makes a claim whose supporting detail is not narrated in the earlier household scene.
edges.label: Tobit’s ancestral advice and Genesis’ household record

edges.basis: Both Gospels connect ordinary activity, Noah’s entry, and sudden destruction to the Son of Man. Matthew develops watchfulness and the unknown hour; Luke pairs Noah with Lot and develops departure, loss, and not turning back.
edges.label: The days of Noah in Matthew and Luke

edges.basis: Genesis narrates water destroying outside life while the ship preserves Noah’s household; 1 Peter carries Noah’s water into a statement about baptism through Christ’s resurrection. The correspondence is explicit, but the passage itself rejects a simple bodily-washing explanation and leaves difficult links open.
edges.label: Flood preservation and baptismal correspondence

edges.basis: Genesis records command and obedience without a sermon; 2 Peter names Noah a preacher of righteousness. The later title is canonical evidence about Noah but cannot be rewritten as speech supplied by Genesis.
edges.label: Noah obeys and later becomes a preacher

edges.basis: 1 Peter places Noah inside a Christ, spirits, water, and baptism sequence; 2 Peter places him inside examples of judgment and deliverance. The shared Noah memory supports different arguments and should not be forced into one explanation.
edges.label: Two apostolic uses of Noah

topic.orientation: Follow Noah from his naming and the violent world around him through warning, ship-building, flood preservation, dry ground, offering, covenant, household fracture, death, and later canonical memory. Keep Noah distinct from the Flood event and the Covenant concept.
